Pregnancy

Ostrich liver in pregnancy: nutrients, risks and better ways to get iron

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Iron needs rise during pregnancy, so it is understandable to look for foods that might prevent or improve anaemia. Ostrich liver may be suggested because it contains iron and other nutrients. Its nutrient content, however, does not make it a recommended pregnancy food.

Should you eat ostrich liver during pregnancy?

The practical advice is to avoid ostrich liver during pregnancy, just as you would avoid other liver and liver products. NHS pregnancy guidance identifies the high vitamin A content of liver as the reason for this restriction. Ostrich liver is not an established exception.

This advice applies throughout pregnancy. Early development is an important reason to be careful about excess preformed vitamin A, but reaching the second or third trimester does not turn liver into a recommended iron treatment. Nor does cooking it thoroughly remove the need to follow the liver-avoidance advice.

You can meet your nutritional needs through other foods and, when appropriate, supplements recommended by your maternity team. If someone suggests liver to treat low iron, ask the team for an alternative plan rather than trying to estimate a safe number of bites.

What the nutrient claims can tell you

Ostrich liver is an organ meat with a similar general appearance and culinary use to other animal livers. It contains protein and minerals. A comparative laboratory study found substantial iron and zinc in its ostrich-liver samples and also measured calcium. That describes food composition; it does not show that eating it improves pregnancy outcomes.

Lists describing this food often also mention vitamin A, folate or vitamin B9, vitamin B12, chromium and copper. Exact amounts should come from a reliable analysis of the relevant food, not be borrowed from beef, sheep or chicken liver. The studies checked for this article do not establish a complete vitamin profile or a dependable amount for every serving.

Calling a food nutrient-dense does not make it the best choice for every person or life stage. An ingredient can supply useful nutrients while also being unsuitable during pregnancy. Claims that ostrich liver is always healthier than red meat or contains a fixed multiple of its iron need more specific evidence.

Health-benefit claims need more than a nutrient list

Nutrition discussions sometimes present ostrich liver as anti-inflammatory or antioxidant, or claim that it strengthens nerves, immunity and resistance to infections. Others promise better memory, learning, eye health or eyesight. The ordinary roles of nutrients in the body do not establish that this particular food produces those benefits when eaten.

More ambitious claims include preventing Alzheimer’s disease, easing gout or rheumatoid-arthritis pain, protecting the heart and treating fatty liver. The food-composition studies reviewed here did not test those outcomes in people. Such claims should not be used as reasons to replace a diagnosed condition’s treatment with liver.

The same distinction applies to claims about treating anaemia, chronic fatigue or low energy, improving skin, reducing hair loss attributed to iron deficiency, strengthening the body, or improving children’s growth and development. Correcting an identified deficiency can be important, but symptoms such as fatigue or hair loss have more than one possible cause. Assessment should identify the problem and guide treatment.

There is no established pregnancy benefit that outweighs the advice to avoid liver. A lack of pregnancy trials is not proof of benefit outside pregnancy, and a long list of possible nutrient functions should not be presented as a list of demonstrated medical effects.

Why vitamin A changes the advice

Vitamin A is needed for normal development, vision and immune function. The concern is excess intake of its preformed form, including retinol and retinyl esters, which is found in animal foods and some supplements. Too much can disrupt fetal development, including development of the eyes, skull and heart.

That does not mean all foods associated with vitamin A should be avoided. Vegetables such as carrots and leafy greens contain provitamin A carotenoids, including beta-carotene, which the body can convert as needed. These foods do not carry the same preformed-vitamin-A concern as liver.

Check supplement labels as well as food choices. Avoid adding retinol-containing supplements or cod-liver oil during pregnancy unless a clinician has specifically advised an appropriate treatment. Take your prescribed or recommended prenatal supplements as directed, and ask a pharmacist if you are unsure which form of vitamin A a label contains.

Fat, cholesterol and other safety questions

Liver is not the same as lean muscle meat. In one study of 24 ostriches, liver fat varied considerably between samples. A general description of ostrich meat as low in fat cannot automatically be applied to every ostrich liver.

Dietary fat, cholesterol, the overall eating pattern and a person’s health all matter when assessing cardiovascular risk. It is too simplistic to say that one serving inevitably raises blood cholesterol or causes heart disease. For pregnancy, the specific liver warning is sufficient reason to choose another food, without making unsupported predictions about an individual meal.

The advice about liver should also not be extended into a claim that every organ has an identical vitamin A content. Heart, kidney and liver differ. Ask about the particular food and local pregnancy guidance rather than assuming either that all offal is equivalent or that another organ is automatically suitable.

Food handling and adequate cooking remain important for animal foods in general. Raw or undercooked meat can cause infection. These food-safety measures address a different risk from the nutrient-related reason for avoiding liver; they do not cancel it.

Getting iron without using liver

Suitable iron sources include appropriately cooked lean meat or poultry, beans, lentils and iron-fortified cereals. A varied diet can combine animal and plant sources according to your preferences. Pairing plant iron with a vitamin C food, such as peppers or citrus fruit, can help its absorption.

If a blood test shows low iron or anaemia, ask what the result means and what treatment is needed. Food choices may support treatment, but established deficiency may require an iron supplement and follow-up. Do not replace a prescribed supplement with liver or add extra iron products without checking the total plan.

Tell your maternity team about troublesome tiredness or other symptoms rather than assuming they must be due to low iron. Also mention supplements, liver powders or capsules and other concentrated products you take. A food sold in capsule form still needs its ingredients and doses assessed.

If you have already eaten some

If you ate a small amount before learning the advice, it does not automatically mean your baby has been harmed. NHS guidance offers reassurance after small accidental amounts of foods normally avoided in pregnancy, while advising you to seek advice if worried or unwell.

Avoid further liver and tell your midwife or clinician roughly how much you ate, when, how often, and whether you also take a vitamin A supplement. Repeated servings or uncertain concentrated products deserve an individual discussion. There is no basis here for guaranteeing that “a few pieces” are safe for everyone or for calculating your baby’s risk from a generic article.

Seek prompt advice if you feel unwell after eating it. Keep the response proportionate: asking for a review of an exposure is different from assuming that a developmental problem has occurred.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pregnancy food guidance advises avoiding liver and liver products because of preformed vitamin A.

Food-composition studies do not establish treatment benefits or pregnancy safety.

Low iron should be assessed and treated through an individual food and supplement plan.

How BeMama can help

Make a short list of the iron-containing foods you enjoy and the supplements you already take. Bring it to your maternity appointment so the plan is practical and avoids duplicate products.

When to seek help

Ask your maternity team about repeated liver intake, uncertain vitamin A doses or symptoms after eating. A small accidental serving does not by itself establish harm.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Avoid ostrich liver during pregnancy rather than using it as an iron remedy.
  • Nutrient content is different from proof that a food treats a disease.
  • Vegetable carotenoids are different from the preformed vitamin A concern in liver.
  • After an accidental serving, seek proportionate individual advice instead of assuming harm or relying on a guaranteed safe portion.

Frequently asked questions

What vitamins and minerals are in ostrich liver?

It contains protein and minerals, with iron and zinc documented in food-composition research. Exact vitamin and mineral amounts vary; a complete profile should not be assumed from another animal’s liver.

Are all the advertised benefits proven?

No. Measurements of nutrients do not prove that ostrich liver treats anaemia, fatigue, fatty liver or arthritis, prevents Alzheimer’s disease, or improves memory and immunity.

What is the main pregnancy concern?

Liver is a concentrated source of preformed vitamin A. Excess intake can harm fetal development, which is why pregnancy guidance advises avoiding liver and liver products.

Can it harm my baby?

Excess preformed vitamin A is a developmental risk, but eating liver once does not establish that harm occurred. Discuss the amount, timing and any supplements with your maternity team if concerned.

Does thorough cooking make it suitable?

No. Cooking is important for infection prevention, but it does not make liver exempt from pregnancy advice about vitamin A.

Can I have a few pieces to satisfy a craving?

There is no established safe portion offered here. Choose an alternative food. If you have already eaten a little, do not assume harm; ask for individual advice if worried.

What can I eat for iron instead?

Appropriately cooked lean meat or poultry, beans, lentils and iron-fortified cereals are options. Follow your maternity team’s supplement plan if you have low iron or anaemia.

Should I avoid carrots because they contain vitamin A?

No. Their vitamin A precursors are carotenoids, which are different from preformed vitamin A in liver. They can remain part of a varied pregnancy diet.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
